On the one hand, they don't really make open world games like this very often. The Bethesda titles have their own appeal in that you can walk around in first person, talk to people, collect plants, make potions.... do quests... it's pretty great.

On the other hand, this is a huge step down from Morrowind. I've always found this game resentful to me as a Morrowind fan. My favorite part of Morrowind? Reading tons of dialogue explaning the story and the world and its history to me. In Skyrim, instead since all the lines are voiced you get only a few lines per person you talk to and they barely explain anything. In Morrowind there were tons of unique books to read, in Skyrim half the books are the same books in Morrowind and the others didn't really grab my attention. In Morrowind casting spells makes you feel extremely powerful, as you can levitate or breathe underwater or walk on water or craft a nuke spell that does 100 damage in every element. In Skyrim, I never cast spells because they just feel so weak and ineffectual. In Morrowind, the factions care who you are, recognize you, will treat you different if you aren't associated with their faction, and you will often have to bribe people to even get them to give you the time of day. Skyrim, everyone will talk to you basically any time.

Pretty much everything I like about Morrowind was removed from this game. It's still fun, there's still enjoyment to be had, but it's just like I talk to an NPC and I'm getting punched in the gut with the longing to hear about their background and their job and their faction and their take on politics....

Also, the dragons that were the main selling point of this game, are the worst part of the game. They fly into cities and torch important NPCs, play keepaway for like 15 minutes at a time so you can't just instagib them like you would be able to otherwise, and they drop stuff way too heavy to ever actually carry around or use. Every time I see a dragon I seriously just want to turn the game off. People make complaints about cliff racers in Morrowind, but imagine cliff racers that will detect you from much further away (we're talking across mountain ranges) and are even harder to hit; you have Skyrim's dragons. It's not even close which is more annoying.

Skyrim is still one of the best open-world RPGs out there, with so much freedom in how you play. Whether you're exploring dungeons, joining factions, crafting gear, or getting distracted by random side quests, there's always something to do. The combat isn't the deepest, but the build variety and exploration more than make up for it. And the mods are even crazier, letting you turn the game into pretty much anything you want. Even after all these years, it's ridiculously easy to lose hundreds of hours in this game.

I've been playing this game since its early days and grew up with it. That's why I'm so attached to it. I bought it twice—first LE, then SE... But now it’s only mods that are keeping it alive, because let’s be honest, the game isn’t anything special these days. The graphics are absolutely awful. And those bugs… I don’t usually notice bugs that much, but there are so many of them—and they’re so game-breaking—that it’s just not fun anymore. Still, thanks to the modding community, Skyrim has perhaps the largest number of mods ever, and thanks to that, you can turn Skyrim into a completely new game that will only crash occasionally. 

Yet Bethesda decided to take the worst possible steps imaginable and simply start brutally bullying this community, which is the very reason Skyrim is still alive. So they’ve decided to release a new update that you’re supposed to buy again? For the third time? Seriously? And what do you get in return? Creation Club mods made by other people? When the internet is full of mods that you can choose for yourself, not based on whether the mod even makes sense in the Skyrim world. They weren’t even able to properly integrate them into the game, so you’ll get mods that aren’t voiced, add items that don’t spawn anywhere in Skyrim, and overlap with existing items. They fixed only a handful of bugs—and created new ones. On top of all that, they keep releasing these tiny updates, every single one of which breaks other people’s mods, so there’s no other way to explain it except that they’re doing it on purpose. So I can’t say a single positive thing about Skyrim as it stands today.

Skyrim: The Greatest and Most Enjoyable Open-World Game Since November 11, 2011
Introduction: A Legendary Journey Through an Unforgettable World
On November 11, 2011, the gaming world changed with the release of The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim, an open-world role-playing game developed by Bethesda Game Studios. From the moment players stepped into the snowy province of Skyrim, they were introduced to a world that felt enormous, mysterious, and full of possibilities. The game offered something that few titles had managed to deliver at the same level: the freedom to explore an entire fantasy world at one's own pace, become almost any kind of character, uncover countless secrets, and create adventures that felt personal rather than predetermined. More than a decade after its original release, Skyrim continues to hold a special place in gaming culture. Its lasting popularity raises an important question: what makes this game so enjoyable that players continue returning to it years after experiencing its world for the first time?
Although many excellent open-world games have been released since 2011, Skyrim remains one of the strongest contenders for the title of the greatest open-world game ever created. Its success cannot be explained by graphics alone, technical perfection, or even the quality of its main storyline. Instead, Skyrim succeeds because its different elements combine to create an experience that is remarkably easy to become immersed in. Exploration is rewarding, the world feels alive with history, character development encourages experimentation, and nearly every journey has the potential to become a memorable adventure. A player can begin the game intending to complete a particular quest and end up spending hours investigating a distant ruin, joining a faction, learning a new skill, or following an unexpected path through the wilderness.
What separates Skyrim from many other games is the sense that the player is not simply completing a developer's checklist. The player is living a second life in a fictional world. There is no single correct way to experience the game, and there is no requirement to follow the main story immediately. Someone can become a powerful warrior, a mysterious assassin, a master thief, an expert mage, a traveling explorer, or a combination of several different archetypes. Every playthrough can feel different because the player decides which opportunities to pursue and which parts of the world to ignore.
This essay argues that Skyrim deserves recognition as one of the best and most enjoyable open-world games since its release on November 11, 2011. Its greatest achievements are its freedom, atmosphere, exploration, role-playing systems, memorable locations, music, replayability, and remarkable ability to make ordinary moments feel like extraordinary adventures. While it has technical flaws and faces serious competition from later games, its overall experience demonstrates why an open world should be measured not only by its size or graphical quality, but also by how strongly it inspires curiosity, imagination, and a desire to return.

 The Freedom to Create Your Own Adventure

One of Skyrim's greatest strengths is the freedom it gives players. Many games feature large maps, but a large map does not automatically create a meaningful open-world experience. A world can contain hundreds of locations and still feel restrictive if players are constantly pushed toward a narrow sequence of objectives. Skyrim takes a different approach by allowing players to make their own decisions about how they want to spend their time.
After the opening sequence, the game introduces the player to a province filled with settlements, mountains, caves, ancient ruins, forests, forts, and hidden locations. The main quest provides a central narrative, but it does not demand constant attention. A player can follow the story, abandon it temporarily, and return whenever they feel ready. This flexibility gives the experience a natural rhythm. There is no need to rush toward the ending when there are so many other things worth discovering.
The freedom to choose a direction is particularly important. A distant mountain might catch the player's attention, or a road might lead toward an unfamiliar settlement. A ruined tower on the horizon could become the destination for the next hour. These decisions may have little to do with the main storyline, yet they are often the moments that make the game memorable. The player explores because something looks interesting, not necessarily because a quest marker demands it.
This design encourages a personal connection to the world. Two people can play Skyrim for dozens of hours and develop completely different stories. One might concentrate on the main quest and become a legendary Dragonborn. Another might spend most of the game stealing valuables, improving equipment, and completing jobs for the Thieves Guild. Someone else might avoid major factions altogether and focus on discovering every corner of the wilderness.
The game does not insist that one approach is more legitimate than another. It accommodates different interests and allows players to define their own goals. This is a major reason Skyrim can appeal to people who enjoy very different kinds of games. Those who love combat can spend their time fighting enemies, while those who enjoy discovery can concentrate on exploration. Players interested in character progression can improve skills, craft equipment, and develop specialized builds.
The result is an experience that feels unusually personal. Skyrim is not simply a story that the player watches unfold. It is a setting in which the player creates a story through decisions, detours, successes, 
and mistakes. This freedom is central to its lasting appeal.
 
An Open World That Rewards Curiosity


Exploration is the heart of Skyrim. The game repeatedly encourages players to investigate unfamiliar places, and it frequently rewards that curiosity with unexpected discoveries. This is one of the most important differences between a world that merely looks large and a world that feels genuinely worth exploring.
In Skyrim, the player can see a distant structure and wonder what lies inside. Approaching it might reveal a bandit camp, a forgotten tomb, a powerful enemy, a hidden treasure, or an entrance to a sprawling underground dungeon. Sometimes the discovery leads to a quest. At other times, it simply provides a fascinating location to investigate. Either outcome makes the journey feel worthwhile.
The placement of locations helps create a continuous sense of possibility. A road rarely feels like nothing more than a route between two objectives. It is an opportunity to encounter something unexpected. A traveler might request assistance, a group of enemies might block a mountain pass, or an unmarked location might appear just beyond a ridge. These interruptions create stories that develop naturally through play.
This kind of exploration is especially satisfying because it respects the player's curiosity. The game does not need to explain every mystery in advance. A strange doorway, a ruined building, or a distant landmark can be enough to inspire investigation. The player supplies the question, and the world provides the opportunity to discover an answer.
Skyrim's dungeons are another important part of this experience. Many contain environmental clues, traps, puzzles, hidden passages, and rewards. Ancient Nordic ruins introduce players to the remnants of a civilization that existed long before the current inhabitants. Dwemer ruins reveal mysterious mechanical structures associated with a lost people whose disappearance remains one of the setting's most intriguing mysteries. Caves and abandoned forts often suggest histories that extend beyond the immediate encounter.

"WAIT! I KNOW YOU!!!" 

10/10 dialogue for a GUARD! For the THIRD GAME IN A ROW! Elder Scrolls continues to be the only game series that can pull me into the world with the fifth entry, Skyrim, teaching me to embrace my Dovahkiin roots. This is hands down my favorite game in the franchise with it containing a certain magically charm often referred to as "Lightning in a Bottle" and it really cannot be understated how true this is. Sure, the world is a little TOO big and there are lots of fields and trees with random events happening either far too often or never enough with a litany of common knowledge bugs and tricks players have come to know over the years that can isolate new-comers to the game but to me, it is more than that. Skyrim is so amazing because it exists beyond its issues and is seen as a whole. Sure devs can make the game super easy and straight forward and linear but our real world is far from those things so why make Tamriel like this? A game with constant dopamine rushes will burn out your brain and cause a crash. When i finally find a sweet roll in Skyrim, whether the first or 10,000th, I'm getting excited and taking it. Caves can feel empty, things repetitive, and towns small because well, towns ARE small! Caves ARE empty! (usually ;) ) and yes, life can get repetitive, that's not Skyrim's fault! 

So why play it? You get so absorbed you as a player begin to exist now not as yourself, but as THE Dragonborn. Maybe for you personally, games can pull you in and you love to roleplay, as do I, but in the end, it is always just a game, no matter how fun or immersed my roleplay is, potentially unlike you. HOWEVER!!! When I play Skyrim... Oh Baby.... its the only time in my life I'm not just moving a controller stick or pressing keys or typing because, as cringe as it may be, I am living my magical and medieval second life. I Loved Skyrim: Anniversary Edition on Steam and mods were all I could have expected and more! <3 Nothing can ever make me feel as if I am doing anything more than playing a game until I load into Skyrim and and ask myself, "what do I WANT to do Today?" because in Skyrim, ESPECIALLY with mods, it is the only time i believe i can do anything I want.
